activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Rosalie ran into the art room. She wanted to paint a big sun. But the paint pots were just red, yellow, and blue.

"Where is orange?" she asked. The sun needed orange! She looked and looked. No orange pot anywhere.

Rosalie dipped her brush in the yellow. She made a yellow dot on her paper. Then she dipped in the red. She put red on top of the yellow dot. She stirred it with her brush.

"Orange!" she shouted. "Red and yellow make orange!" That was true. She had made a brand new colour all by herself.

She painted her sun. It was big and orange and bright. Then she wanted purple grapes. She tried red and blue together. Purple! She clapped her hands.

Her teacher smiled. Rosalie pointed at her paper. "Look what I made!" she said.

Later, her father came to pick her up. Rosalie held up the painting. "Can we write my name on it?" she asked. Her father found a crayon. He wrote R-O-S-A-L-I-E at the top.

"Sun day!" Rosalie said, and she hugged the painting tight.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Lena was at daycare. Teacher Mia had a big bag. Out came library books. "We can borrow these," said Teacher Mia. "We take them home. Then we bring them back, so other kids can read them too."

Lena picked a book about a cat. She held the book. She turned the pages. The cat kicked a ball on page two. The cat ate with a spoon on page four. Lena pointed at the marks on the page. "Cat," she said. The words meant cat.

Lena hugged the book. "I want to keep it forever," she said. "The library needs it back," said Teacher Mia. Lena looked at the book. She looked at her friend Sam. Sam wanted the cat book too. Lena gave Sam the book. "You read it now," she said. "Then it goes back to the library." Sam opened the front cover. "Read it front to back," said Lena. Sam turned page one.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Naomi had a library book. It was about a beautiful dragon. She hugged it at bedtime. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

Mama shook her head. "We take it back on Friday. Then other kids can read it too."

Naomi hid the book under her pillow. The dragon could live with her! She counted the pages. One, two, three, four. The words on each page said what the dragon did. She read them front to back. The last page said, "The dragon flies away."

Naomi heard a tiny sound. Tap, tap. The book was wiggling! "The dragon wants to go fly," she said. "That is why she is tapping."

In the morning, Naomi did not forget. She carried the book through the kitchen. She put it right in her bag. "Fly, dragon," she whispered. "I will get a new dragon book soon."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Florence stood in the backyard. She held a small beanbag in her hand. A big hoop lay on the grass. She wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Florence threw the beanbag. The wind began to blow. The beanbag sailed up and then tipped sideways. It fell in the grass, far from the hoop. Florence got the beanbag and tried again. The wind blew once more. The beanbag tipped away again.

Florence watched the leaves on the tree. When the leaves hung still, she threw. The beanbag flew straight and dropped right into the hoop. "The wind pushed it," said Florence. "Now the wind is asleep."

Then Dad rolled a big ball to her. Florence held out one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. She put both hands out, close together. Dad rolled the ball again. Florence caught it with her two hands. "I got it!" she said. Just then a butterfly landed right on the hoop. Florence held her ball and smiled. "Come play too," she said.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jules wanted a snack. He saw a big watermelon on the table. "Can I have some?" he asked. Mama said, "Yes, but it is late. Let us hurry."

Jules used his eyes to look at the watermelon. It was green on the outside. "What is inside?" he asked. "Knock on it and listen," said Mama. Jules knocked on the top with his knuckles. Knock, knock! He heard a deep sound. "It sounds full!" he said.

Mama cut the watermelon. Jules used his nose to smell it. It smelled sweet. His mouth got watery. He took a big bite. His tongue tasted the juicy fruit. "So sweet!" he said. The juice ran down his chin. He touched the rind with his fingers. It was smooth and hard.

"Why did we knock on it?" Jules asked. Mama said, "A ripe one sounds deep. A bad one sounds dull." Jules knocked again. Deep sound. Ripe! He ate one more piece and licked his fingers.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Evan stood at the gate of the school playground. His backpack felt light on his back. Mom gave him a hug and waved goodbye.

Evan wanted to play on the slide. But he did not know any kids. He stood still. His zipper got stuck on his jacket. He pulled and pulled. Then a girl came over. She looked at the tag on his backpack. It said his name in big letters. "Hi, Evan," she said. "I am Mia." Evan smiled big.

The teacher blew a whistle. It was time for a break and a snack. Evan sat with Mia under a tree. He shared his crackers. The sun made warm light on the grass. Evan looked at Mia's tag. It said her name too. He pointed at it. "Mia," he said. "The tag tells me your name!" Mia laughed and clapped. "Come on," she said. "Let's go to the slide!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Milo was at Grandma's house. Grandma was painting at her table. "This flower is blue," she said. "But my blue paint is all gone."

Milo wanted to help. He hurried to the paint shelf. He found a jar with blue on the lid. But it was empty. He found a jar with yellow paint. That one was full.

Milo climbed on his chair. He squeezed the yellow paint into a cup. He added a drop of blue from Grandma's little tube. The colors swirled in the cup. Milo stirred with a smooth wooden stick.

The paint turned green! Milo looked and looked. "Yellow and blue make green," he said. "That is why Grandma has no green flower."

Grandma laughed and clapped. "Paint me a green leaf, Milo." Milo made a big green leaf. Then he made three more. Grandma hung them on the wall.

After all that work, Milo was sleepy. Grandma made him a soft bed for his nap. "You helped me today," she said. She tucked the blanket up to his chin. Milo yawned. "Yellow and blue make green," he said. Grandma kissed his head. "Good night, my helper."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Elizabeth wanted to wear her bear pajamas tonight. But where were they? She looked under her bed. She saw one sock. She looked in her toy box. She saw two blocks. She looked in the bathtub. She saw her yellow duck.

Then Elizabeth touched the bathtub. It was wet. "Hmm," she said. "The pajamas are not here. The bathtub is wet. Mommy washed clothes today!" Elizabeth ran to the laundry basket. She looked inside. She saw three shirts, two towels and her bear pajamas!

But the pajamas were damp. Mommy hung them near the warm heater. Elizabeth waited. She zipped up her doll's coat while she waited. At last the pajamas were dry and warm. She put them on. She rubbed her eye, big and sleepy. Mommy tucked her in, snug and safe. "Wet clothes dry by the heater," said Elizabeth. "Goodnight, bear."

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Iris was at school. She painted a big red apple at the art table. Then the teacher rang a little bell. "Snack time," said the teacher. Iris wanted the crunchy crackers. She ran to the door of the snack room.

The teacher held up her hand. "Look at your hands, Iris," she said. Iris looked. There was red paint on her hands. "Are they dirty?" asked Iris. "Yes, they are," said the teacher. "So we wash them first."

Iris went to the sink. She turned on the water. She rubbed the soap. Bubbles grew and grew. Pop, pop, pop. Iris laughed. She had not seen so many bubbles. The paint went down the drain. Now her hands were clean.

Iris washed and washed until they sparkled. She walked to the snack room and got her crackers. She took a big bite. Crunch, crunch, crunch. "The paint is gone," said Iris. "Because I washed my hands, my crackers stay clean." She held one up to the teacher. "A clean cracker for you," said Iris.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Leo put seeds in a pot on the balcony. He patted the dirt down flat. Then he waited. He waited all day. Nothing came up.

"Hello, little seed," said Leo. "Wake up!"

His friend Mia lived next door. She leaned over the railing. "Seeds need water," she said. "Did you give it a drink?"

Leo ran to the kitchen. He filled a small orange cup. He poured the water on the dirt. "There," he said. "Now you can work, little seed."

Every morning Leo gave the pot water from the orange cup. One day a green nose poked out of the dirt. Then two little leaves stood up.

"The water helped you," said Leo. "No water, no seed. Water, and up you pop!"

Mia laughed from her balcony. "You are a good farmer, Leo."

Leo held up his cup. "More water, please!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexis was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home today. Her name was Rosie.

Rosie slept in a little basket. Then Rosie woke up. She cried and cried. "She is mean," said Alexis. "She is loud!" Grandma smiled. "Babies cannot talk," she said. "Crying is how she talks."

Grandma held Rosie near Alexis. Rosie kept crying. Grandma said, "Try one thing at a time." Alexis gave Rosie a soft blanket. Rosie still cried. Alexis patted Rosie's head. Rosie still cried. Then Alexis put his finger near Rosie's hand. Rosie grabbed it and stopped.

"She stopped because I gave her my finger," said Alexis. "She wanted to hold on." Grandma laughed. "Yes, it worked. She wanted to hold something warm."

Dad came in with milk in a small bottle. "Rosie is hungry too," he said. "You can help." Alexis sat very still. Dad let Alexis hold the bottle. Rosie drank and drank.

"You are a good big brother," said Dad. "You are like her teacher." Alexis grinned. "Rosie, I will show you everything. But not my toy cars. Those are mine." Rosie made a small burp. Alexis laughed so loud that the cat ran under the chair.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Aaron sat on Grandma's big red blanket. "Let's play a game," said Grandma. "Tell me your five senses."

Aaron frowned. "I don't know them all." He wanted to get it right.

Grandma rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Aaron covered his ears. "That is loud!" he said. "My ears hear it!" Grandma smiled. "Ears are one," she said.

Next she held up a yellow lemon. Aaron sniffed it. "Pee-yew! My nose smells it!" "Noses are two," said Grandma. Aaron licked his lips. "My tongue tastes. Three!"

Grandma gave him a soft kitten. Aaron petted its warm fur. "My hands feel it. Four!" Then he looked out the window. He saw a blue bird. "My eyes see it. Five!" he shouted.

"You said them all," said Grandma. "Ears, nose, tongue, hands, eyes." Aaron clapped his hands. He said the list again, all by himself. He got none of them wrong this time.

"Say it once more," said Grandma. Aaron took a big breath. "Ears, nose, tongue, hands, eyes!" The kitten purred in his lap, and Aaron giggled.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Jasper stood at the little table in his classroom. Ten number cards lay in a box. His teacher had said, "Put them in a row, one to ten."

Jasper laid the cards out. One, two, three, four, five, six. He put the next card down. Eight, then nine, then ten. He looked at his row. It felt wrong.

"I know," said Jasper. "Eight comes after seven. A card is missing." He looked under the table. He looked by the doll home in the corner. There it was, the seven card, tucked in a tiny bed.

Jasper picked it up and slid it in its place. Now the row went one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. He counted it out loud. It sounded just like the song.

"Seven was hiding," said Jasper. "That is why my row was broken."

His teacher smiled. "Now it is all better."

Jasper sang the counting song all the way to the shelf.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe sat in a big chair at the clinic. Her mom held her hand. A friendly nurse named Sam came in with a small tray. Zoe saw the tiny needle and made her arm stiff like a rock.

"Will it hurt a lot?" Zoe asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Sam. "Try to let your arm go soft. A tight arm hurts more. A soft arm hurts less."

Zoe looked at her stiff arm. She made a fist. Then she tried to let it go soft, like a sleepy cat. Her arm felt wobbly and loose.

Sam touched the soft skin. "That is just right," he said. "Look out the window while I count."

Outside the window, Zoe saw a garden with red flowers. A bee flew from one flower to another. Zoe kept looking at the bee. She kept her arm soft.

"One, two, three," said Sam. "All done!"

"That was it?" asked Zoe. "That was just a little pinch!"

The tight arm would have hurt more. The soft arm hurt less. Zoe had found that out all by herself.

Sam put a happy bandage on her arm. "You were brave," he said.

"Can I open the sticker box?" Zoe asked. She picked a star sticker and stuck it on her shirt. "I want to show the garden bee," she said, waving from the window.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson woke up hungry. "I want toast," he said. Mom put bread in the toaster. Jaxson watched. He waited. He waited some more. "Is it time?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mom. Then the toaster went pop! The bread jumped up, hot and brown. "The bread popped because it got hot!" said Jaxson. He laughed. "Pop, pop, pop!"

Jaxson ate his toast. It was warm and yummy. He got some crumbs on the floor. Mom handed him a little brush. "Let's make the floor tidy," she said. Jaxson brushed the crumbs away. "Tidy floor!" he said. "Tidy boy," said Mom, and she kissed his head.

After breakfast came a bath. Jaxson splashed and played with his duck. Then Dad helped him get dressed. "Where are your socks?" Dad asked. Jaxson looked. One sock was under the table. One sock was in the toy box. "You silly socks!" said Jaxson. "Come here!" He put them on his feet, one by one. "Warm toes," he said. Dad called out, "Story time, Jaxson!" Jaxson ran to the couch. He held his duck. "Read the duck story," he said. Dad opened the book. "Once there was a little duck," he read. Jaxson snuggled close, and his warm toes wiggled.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Olivier ran to Grandpa's house. He wanted his little red car. But the car was gone. "Where did you go?" Olivier called. "Oh car, you are so naughty!"

Grandpa was in the garden. "Where did you play with it last?" he asked. Olivier thought hard. He looked at the park across the fence. "I pushed the car near the park," he said. So Olivier looked by the fence. He looked in the grass. No car there.

Then Olivier thought again. The car was small. Small things can hide in big places. "My toy went where I went," he said. So he walked his own steps. Through the gate. Past the big chair. Then to his blanket for nap time. He lifted a corner. There was the red car, tucked under the blanket! "The car was cold, so it hid!" Olivier called. Grandpa laughed. Olivier rolled the car down his knee. Vroom, all the way to Grandpa's slipper.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Max put on his big blue apron. It went down to his toes. Today he would make pancakes for his family. One, two, three, mix! That was his job.

Outside, the rain went tap, tap, tap on the window. Inside, Max looked into his bowl. The batter was lumpy. Big lumps. Little lumps. Lumpy, lumpy, lumpy. His tummy said, "I want smooth pancakes!"

So Max stirred. One, two, three, mix! The lumps got smaller. He stirred more. One, two, three, mix! The lumps went away. "The lumps went away because I mixed!" said Max.

The teacher poured the batter into the hot pan. Sizzle, sizzle! Then bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop. Max flipped the pancake high. It did a little jump.

At last the family came to eat. Max said, "I mixed it smooth!" Daddy took a big bite. Mama took a big bite. Baby took a tiny bite. Max counted the empty plates. One, two, three! Then he patted his full tummy and said, "More pancakes, please!"

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Joshua went to the park with his blue bunny. He put bunny down on the grass. Then he ran to play ball with his dad. The ball bounced high. Joshua laughed and kicked it back. It was not too hard for him. He was getting good at it.

Then Joshua looked for bunny. Bunny was gone! Joshua wanted to cry, but he took a big breath. He thought and thought. "I played ball here first," he said. "Bunny was in the soft grass near the swings." He walked back to the swings. He looked down low, near his feet. There was bunny, hiding in the tall green grass! Joshua hugged bunny tight.

A little girl came by. "Do you want to share my ball?" she asked. Joshua smiled. "Yes, please," he said. He put bunny safe in his bag. Then he kicked the ball far, far up into the sky.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Arthur rode the city bus with his red bus. "Where did you go?" he asked. Snow fell on the windows. Arthur peeked under his seat. Only dirt and an old ticket lived there.

He thought and thought. "I had my red bus when we got on," he said. "The bus stopped. I slid forward." So his red bus slid too! Arthur looked under the seat behind him. There it was, by a gum wrapper. "You slid back when the bus stopped!" he said. He picked it up and held it tight.

Arthur tried a little test. He put the red bus on his knee. The bus stopped again. The red bus slid, just a little. "It moves because the big bus stops!" said Arthur. "That is so neat." The snow kept falling, and Arthur held his red bus all the way home.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Alexander woke up and sniffed the air. Something smelled sweet! He used his nose to smell it. Was it cookies? He ran to the kitchen on his little feet.

Mom was baking cookies. "These are for the school sale," she said. "We will sell them at the big table." Alexander wanted a cookie now. But the cookies were too hot to touch. He touched one with his finger and pulled it back fast. "Ow! Hot!" His fingers told him it was hot.

Then he heard a sound outside. His ears heard a funny sound. "Hoo! Hoo!" He looked out with his eyes. It was an owl in the tree! The owl was awake at night. That was funny, because Alexander slept at night.

Mom gave him a warm cookie. He put it in his mouth. His tongue tasted sugar and butter. It was so good! Alexander said, "My nose found the cookies first. My nose knew before my eyes!" Mom laughed and handed him a glass of milk.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story: Ibrahim woke up in his small bed. The sun was up too. He wanted to play outside with his red fire truck. "First we get dressed," said Mama. One sock, two socks. One shoe, two shoes. Ibrahim pulled his shirt too fast. Rip! The sleeve tore a little. "Oops," he said. "Slow hands next time," said Mama. She helped him put on a good blue shirt. Then she made warm toast. Ibrahim ate it all up. But then he stepped in a puddle by the sink. His socks got wet. He tried to put his shoes on. The wet socks felt cold and squishy. "Wet socks, cold toes," said Ibrahim. Mama dried his feet with a soft towel. One dry foot, two dry feet. New socks went on. Shoes went on. Ibrahim hugged Mama and ran outside with his fire truck. "The wheels go fast," he called.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Edouard was alone in the playroom. He wanted to count his blocks. "One, two, three," he sang. Then he stopped. What came next?

He tried, "One, two, three, seven!" That felt wrong. He frowned at the blocks.

Then he remembered the counting song. He loved that song! He sang it out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The words came out in a line, one after another.

"Now I know!" said Edouard. He touched each block as he sang. "One, two, three!" Three blocks! The numbers only worked when they came in order. That was why his trick had gone wrong.

He turned to the toy cars next. A car had dirt on its wheel. He wiped it clean. Then he counted the cars, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five!"

"Ten cars!" he sang at the end. He ran to show his mother. "Mama, listen! One, two, three, four, five!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Eliana wanted the big red pencil. Her brother Sam had it. "My turn first," said Sam. "Then you." Eliana stamped her foot. It was hard to wait. The pencil was so red and shiny.

Mama sat down next to them. "You can use the timer," she said. She turned the dial. It went tick, tick, tick. Eliana watched the little hand go around. She smelled the orange peel Mama was peeling. Then the bell rang, ding! Sam gave her the pencil. "Your turn," he said. Eliana drew a big cat with whiskers.

The bell rang again. Eliana did not want to stop. But then she thought, "Sam waited for me. Now I wait too." She gave Sam the pencil. He smiled. "Your cat is funny," he said. Then he added a hat on the cat. Eliana laughed. "I wish I had a hat too," she said. Mama set the timer again. Tick, tick, tick.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Nathan stood by the little pool near the lake. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But every time he put his face in, water went up his nose. Then he coughed and sat on the step.

"You can blow out," said his friend Mia. She put her face in the water. Bubbles came out of her nose. Nathan watched. Mia lifted her head. "See? Bubbles," she said. Nathan took a big breath. He put his face down. He blew bubbles out of his nose. No water went in. He did not cough. He lifted his head and laughed. "The water stays out when I blow!" he said.

Across the lake, a brown cow drank at the edge. A duck paddled by. Nathan's mom waved from her towel. "I did it!" Nathan called. He felt very happy. He put his face in again. More bubbles, no cough. He kicked his legs behind him, splashing small waves. "Tomorrow I will swim all the way to the rope," he said. The sun was warm on his wet head, and he blew one more big bubble.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Ten cookies sat on a big plate. Mom said, "Count them. Then you get the one from the bigger pile!"

Oliver counted from the left. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Then he counted from the right. "One, two, three..." The last number was ten again! "Mom! Ten from this side too! Ten both ways!"

"You got it," said Mom. "Ten cookies, no matter where you start."

A small bee buzzed at the window. Oliver laughed at the busy bee. He picked the soft cookie with the most chips. He counted them. "Nine chips!"

Oliver took a big bite. It was soft and sweet. He did not cry when a crumb fell. He just grabbed a napkin.

"Tomorrow I count my toy cars," he said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Dad put down a big orange bowl of soup. "We say our blessing first," said Dad. Emmett wanted to say it all by himself.

"Fold your hands," said Dad. "Close your eyes. Then repeat after me." Emmett folded his hands. He closed his eyes. It was dark! He could not see Dad at all. But he could hear Dad's voice, nice and slow.

"Thank you for our food," said Dad. "Thank you for our food," said Emmett. "Thank you for our family," said Dad. "Thank you for our family," said Emmett.

Dad clapped. "You said the whole blessing!" Emmett opened his eyes. He looked at Dad, then at Mom, then at his orange soup. "When my eyes are closed, my ears work better!" said Emmett. Dad laughed. "I like that," he said. Mom smiled and picked up her spoon.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Zachary wanted to draw a cat for Mom. The cat would be orange. He saw the tablet in the basket by the big chair.

He tapped the screen once. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark and quiet. Zachary tapped it again. Still nothing. He sat down on the rug and thought.

"How does it wake up?" he asked. Then he remembered. Daddy held the little round button. Zachary found the button. He pushed it and held it. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen grew bright. It was on!

Zachary was so happy he almost forgot to sit still. He looked at the little pictures. One had a paintbrush on it. He tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. He picked orange. He drew a big cat with a long tail. He drew it fast because he was excited. Then he drank some juice from his cup. He drew tiny whiskers too.

Mom came in. "Is the tablet all done now?" she asked. "Yes," said Zachary. He pressed the round button and held it. The screen went dark again. "The button makes it sleep," he said. He put the tablet back in the basket, all by himself. He carried his orange cat to Mom.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Mila was going on a trip. Her family would sleep in a tent. There were no plugs at the campsite. Mila did not know that yet.

She put her little lamp in the car. She put her teddy bear in too. At the campsite, the sky got dark. Mila pressed the button on her lamp. The lamp stayed dark. She pressed it again. Still dark.

"There are no plugs here," said Mama. "The lamp needs a plug. A flashlight needs batteries."

Dad gave Mila a flashlight. It had batteries inside. Mila pressed the button. The light came on! It made a bright circle on the tent wall. The lamp was dark because it had no plug. The flashlight was bright because it had batteries.

Mila put the lamp back in the car. She held the flashlight all night.

"I will bring you next time," she told the lamp.

Teddy sat by her feet. Mila felt proud. She fell asleep in the soft glow.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Joshua stood near the big piano in the music room. He wanted to play a real song. He hit the keys very hard. The sound was loud and bumpy. It sounded like a car horn. Joshua did not like it. "I can't do it," he said. Miss Rosa was near him. She smiled. "Watch my hands," she said. She touched the keys soft and slow. The song came out pretty.

Joshua tried again. He hit the keys soft and slow too. Now the song sounded nice. "Soft hands make a nice song," said Joshua. He played it again. Soft and slow, soft and slow. Miss Rosa clapped. Joshua laughed and played some more. Then he stopped and put his small hand on top of hers. "You play with me," he said.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Charles got on the big bus with Grandma. He held his sleepy bunny by its long string. The bunny was soft and warm.

The bus went bump, bump. Charles sat down. "Where is bunny?" he said. His hands were empty. The string was gone too. Charles wanted to cry.

Grandma said, "Let us look where you sat." They walked back. Charles got on his knees. He peeked under the seat. The bunny had fallen down. It was hiding by a shoe. "Lost things stay where they drop," said Charles. He pulled the string, and out came the bunny.

A girl nearby smiled at him. She had thrown her ball under her seat too. It rolled out to his feet. He picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," she said. Charles hugged his bunny tight. The bus went bump, bump, all the way home.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Nova sat at the craft table at camp. She was making a picture for her old teddy bear, the toy she loved best. She wanted to cover it with glitter.

She squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. One dot, two dots, ten dots, a hundred dots! The paper got very wet. Then the paper tore. A big hole sat right in the middle of her bear.

"Oh no," said Nova. "My bear has a tummy hole."

Her friend Sam peeked over. "Too much glue makes the paper soggy," he said. "Then it rips."

Nova tried again on new paper. This time she made little dots. Dot, dot, dot. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then she shook the glitter on top. The glitter snowed down over her bear like sparkly snowflakes.

The paper stayed whole. The bear shined.

Nova held it up to Sam. "Look! Little dots, no hole," she said.

Sam clapped his hands. "The best bear at camp," he said.

Nova gave the picture a hug, and a bit of glitter snowed onto her nose.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Sofia went to the bank with her dad. It was cold outside. Dad said, "Put on your coat, please."

Sofa pushed her arms in. The coat was on. Now came the zipper. She pulled the zipper up, up, up. But the zipper did not move. The two sides would not join. "Hmm," said Sofia. "Why won't you zip?"

She looked down at the bottom of her coat. The two sides were apart there. What if the bottom had to come together first? Sofia pinched the bottom of the zipper with her fingers. She held it tight. Then she pulled the little tag. The zipper went zzzzzip, all the way up! "It works when the bottom is together," said Sofia. "That is why!"

At the bank, warm air seemed to float around her. Sofia held her coat closed so it would not fall open. Outside after, the cold wind blew. But her coat was not weak against it. The zipper stayed shut.

"Look, Dad," said Sofia. "I did it all by myself." Dad smiled and gave her a big hug.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Luca was at the farm. He had small seeds in his hand. "One for the dirt, two for the dirt, three for the dirt," he said. He patted the dirt on top.

Luca waited. He looked and looked. Nothing grew. He asked his grandpa, "Why won't my seeds grow?" Grandpa just said, "Seeds need water, every day."

So Luca got the little blue watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Drip, drip, drip. The water went down into the ground. He did it each morning. One can, two cans, splash.

A naughty rabbit came near. It sniffed at the dirt. Luca clapped his hands. "Go away, rabbit. That is my garden." The rabbit hopped off to eat grass.

One morning, Luca saw green tips. Tiny leaves pushed up. "The water helped the seeds," he said. "They grew because I watered them."

Grandpa took a picture of Luca by the little plants. Luca smiled big. Later they went to the pond. Grandpa tried to fish. Luca waved at his garden. "Grow, grow, grow," he said softly. The little leaves were still there, waving back in the wind.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Amira ran to math club. She was ready to play. On the table sat two buckets of blocks. One bucket was red. One bucket was blue.

"Which bucket has more?" asked Mr. Tom.

Amira hoped the red bucket had more. It looked big. But she wanted to know for sure. She pulled out the red blocks. She counted them. "One, two, three, four, five." Five! The last number she said was five.

Then she tried again. This time she started at the other end. "One, two, three, four, five." Five again!

"It is the same," said Amira. "I started there, and then there. Both times, five."

She counted the blue blocks too. "One, two, three, four." Only four.

"The red bucket has more!" said Amira. She smiled big. "Five is more than four."

"Good counting," said Mr. Tom. Amira stacked the five red blocks into a tall tower.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Rowan runs to the swings at the playground. He wants the red swing most of all. But a big girl is on it. Rowan waits. One swing, two swings, three swings go back and forth.

The girl jumps off. Rowan runs fast. Then a small boy bumps him. The boy falls down on the soft wood chips. Rowan feels scared that the boy will cry. "Sorry," Rowan says. He helps the boy up. The boy smiles. "Thank you," the boy says.

Now the red swing is free. Rowan climbs on. But he cannot make the swing go. He kicks his legs hard. The swing still stops. A lady walks over. "Can you push me, please?" Rowan asks her. The lady pushes gently. The swing goes up, up, up.

"Thank you," Rowan calls. He laughs in the wind. He tells the lady, "You pushed, so I went high. One push, one big swing!" The lady laughs too. "Again, please," says Rowan. The swing goes up once more.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Kinsley woke up and looked out the window. It was snowing outside. Big soft flakes snowed down on the grass. "Mommy, can we paint today?" she asked. "Yes," said Mommy. "But first I make tea."

Mommy put the kettle on the stove. The stove got hot. Kinsley reached up her hand. Mommy held her fingers back. "Hot things can hurt," Mommy said. Kinsley pulled her hand down fast. She touched the cold window instead. The glass felt cool on her fingers.

Kinsley picked one spot to sit. It was close to Mommy. She could see Mommy and the kettle too. She opened her jar of paint. The red paint was her best one. She made a picture of the snow. White dots went all over the page. She looked at the stove again. The kettle began to sing. Steam came out, and Mommy moved it away.

"I stayed close to you," said Kinsley. Mommy kissed her head. "That is true," said Mommy. "Now let me see that snow picture."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Wesley wanted his rubber duck. The duck was not in the tub. He looked with his eyes. He saw soap and a towel. No duck.

Then he heard a little squeak with his ears. The sound came from under the sink. Wesley bent down. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled toothpaste. The duck was by the toothpaste cup.

He reached with his hands and touched the duck. It was smooth and warm. "Found you," he said.

Mom filled the tub. Wesley put his toes in and touched the warm water. He brushed his teeth and chewed the little toothbrush softly. Then he sat up straight in the water and held the duck high.

"Squeak, squeak," said the duck. "Splash time," said Wesley.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Paisley had a library book about a funny red fox. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight.

Mama sat on the bed. "Show me your book," she said. Paisley opened the front cover. The words there said PAISLEY. "That word is my name!" she said. Mama smiled. She turned the pages one by one, from the front to the back. The words told about the fox. "The words talk to you," said Paisley. "Words say things."

Then Mama showed her a paper card. It had words on it too. "The card says take the book back," said Mama. "Other kids at school want to read the fox book too." Paisley pouted. But then she thought about her friends. They could read the fox after her.

"Tomorrow we take it back," said Paisley. "Then we get a new book."

Mama tucked her in. Paisley patted the fox book one more time.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Zayn put on his red shoes all by himself. "We need shoes for the library," he said. "Silly, the library is not outside," said Mama. Zayn giggled. "My toes like shoes."

At the desk, a kind man gave Zayn a little card. It had his name on it. Zayn picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. He held it tight. "Mine forever!" he said.

At home, Zayn hid the book under his bed. But the next week, the man called. The book had to go back so other kids could read it too. Zayn frowned, then smiled. "I will bring it back. Then I get a new one!" He zipped up his shoes. "Library day!"

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Miles stood in the pool changing room. He put on his little swimsuit. His towel had a big owl on it. The owl looked at him with round eyes.

"Time for swim class," said Dad.

Miles had a problem. Last week, water went up his nose. It hurt. He did not like that. "Dad, will water go in my nose again?" he asked.

"Let's see," said Dad. They walked out to the pool. The water was blue and shiny. Coach Amy held Miles's hands. "Now put your face in the water," she said. "Blow out like a dragon."

Miles put his face in. He blew bubbles. Bloop, bloop, bloop. He lifted his head. No water in his nose! He blew air out, so water could not get in. "Dad! I blew bubbles and my nose is dry!"

"Good try, Miles," said Dad. "One more time?"

Miles put his face in again. Bloop, bloop, bloop. He came up laughing. Then he bumped into a girl with his elbow. "Sorry," said Miles. The girl smiled.

At the end, Miles sat on the step. His owl towel was warm and soft. "I can do it," he said. "I blow out, and the water stays out. Watch me next time!"
